name: The Slagwind Meridian

detectability.signature: A persistent gamma and neutron hum with a faint thermal shimmer; sensors paint it as a slow amber haze against the starfield.

proximity: Dosimeters begin climbing steadily even with shields raised
Starlight seen through the field takes on a faint amber smear
contact: Unshielded crew absorb a year's safe dose within minutes
Solid-state electronics suffer cumulative bit-flips and sensor dropouts
prolonged_exposure: Hull composites embrittle as crystalline lattices degrade under neutron flux
Crew radiation sickness becomes inevitable without heavy shielding

phenomena: Radiation spikes at irregular intervals along the band's densest filaments
Electromagnetic interference patterns warbling across comm channels
A visible amber glow where the field intersects interstellar dust
hazards: Radiation exposure exceeding safe limits outside shielded compartments
Navigation system failure from cumulative electronic degradation
opportunities: Rare element concentration: transuranic isotopes precipitate in the band's calm pockets
Data valuable to scientific institutions studying long-lived radiation belts
known_incidents: The survey cutter Halcyon Step spent nine hours inside the meridian in 2411; her crew survived, but the ship was written off as radiologically unsalvageable
description: The Slagwind Meridian is a slow river of residual radiation, an irregular band tens of thousands of kilometers thick that glows a dull furnace-amber wherever it meets drifting dust. To the naked eye it looks like heat shimmer frozen in vacuum, a slag-colored veil stretched across half a system. Sensors register its approach long before the glow resolves, as a rising whisper of gamma counts.

The field drifts along a broad arc at a steady crawl, thickening into hot filaments and thinning into navigable pockets on a semi-predictable schedule that charters update quarterly. Crossing at a filament's worst means dosimeters redlining within minutes, while a well-timed transit through a pocket costs little more than some scrambled telemetry. Ships that linger find their hulls slowly embrittling, like metal left too near a forge.

Independent prospectors discovered the meridian while chasing anomalous isotope readings from a dead prospector beacon, and the survey cutter Halcyon Step confirmed its lethality at cost nine years later. The band's calm pockets concentrate transuranic isotopes shed by some ancient cataclysm, making it one of the richest unworked deposits in the sector. Salvage law treats the interior as a graveyard boundary; insurance treats it as a dare.

Today the meridian is worked only by shielded drone trains and the occasional fool in a hardened hull, both of which file flight plans the insurers refuse to bless. Research stations ring its perimeter, listening to the field's slow fluctuations for clues to the explosion that seeded it. Every charter pilot learns the pocket map by heart, because the Slagwind forgives the quick and digests the slow.
